title: The moon
hookLine: some sight the moon locally, some follow another country, some use calculation

lines: EID MORNING, THE CHAT IS ARGUING.
cards: Eid morning, and the group chat is arguing. One cousin is already in new clothes, posting photos from the mosque. Another is still fasting, because her mosque says the month has one more day.

A third says his community decided weeks ago, by the numbers. Same city, same family, same Ramadan, and two different Eids. It all comes from one question about a crescent, answered more than one way.

teach.b: The Islamic months follow the moon, and the Qur'an says of the new moons, in Pickthall's words, "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage."
A month begins with the thin crescent, the hilal, just after sunset.

In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it, and if it's hidden from you, complete the month as thirty days. Seeing is at the heart of it.
So, the first question: whose seeing? In Sahih Muslim, Kurayb travels from Syria to Medina. In Syria, he says, people saw the new moon on Friday night and began fasting.

Ibn Abbas, in Medina, answers that they saw it on Saturday night and will keep counting by their own sighting. This is how we were told, he says. Some scholars read that as each region sighting its own moon.

Others say one sighting anywhere binds everyone who hears of it, so some communities follow another country's announcement. The second question: what counts as seeing? Some jurists say an eye on the horizon, nothing else.

Others answer that astronomers can now say ahead of time when the crescent will be born and when it can be seen, and that a reliable calculation can stand in for the eye, or at least rule out a mistaken sighting.
Some councils announce the dates far in advance. So the family chat is arguing over three readings of one sentence about a crescent.

how: Mosques and councils start the Islamic months, including Ramadan and the Eids, by one of several methods: a local sighting of the crescent, following another country's announced sighting, or astronomical calculation.

o: the full moon that marks the middle of each Islamic month
the new crescent that begins each month, sighted or calculated
a festival held on the last night of the fasting month

p: complete the month as thirty days

s: the Islamic months follow the moon
the Qur'an calls the new moons fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage.
in the report in Sahih Muslim, Ibn Abbas switched to Syria's sighting
he kept Medina's own sighting and said, this is how we were told.
two Eids in one city means someone made a mistake
it comes from honest differences: local sighting, another country's sighting, or calculation.

games.q: you're Ibn Abbas in Medina. Kurayb arrives: Syria saw the new moon a night before you did. do you change your count?
o: no, keep counting by Medina's own sighting.
games.why: Ibn Abbas keeps Medina's sighting and says, this is how we were told. some scholars read local sighting into it; others still hold one sighting can bind everyone who hears of it.

practice: Picture the new crescent: a thin silver edge low in the west after sunset, the way it looks to anyone waiting for it. Breathe slowly while you hold it.
If you have a mosque, you might ask yourself which way it counts: its own sighting, another country's announcement, or calculation.

wordCard.voice: The moon. The new crescent begins each Islamic month; some sight it locally, some follow another country's sighting, some use calculation. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the new crescent moon that begins a month.

carryVoice: Your line: which moon? One crescent, more than one honest count, and one family. See you tomorrow.
